proposal.problem: The claim asserts that adding 20 ms delay changes TCP flow completion time under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions, but the directionality of the delay, transfer size, and CCA are unspecified, preventing a complete frozen protocol.
proposal.question: Does adding 20 ms of emulated delay (vs. 0 ms baseline) produce a measurable difference in TCP flow completion time under a fixed bottleneck in a netem emulation?

proposal.conditions: Two conditions: (A) 0 ms added delay, (B) 20 ms added delay. All other parameters — bottleneck rate, buffer size, CCA, file size, number of clients — held constant across conditions.
proposal.related_work: Emulated network testbeds using Linux netem are a standard approach for controlled TCP performance studies. Delay effects on flow completion time are well-studied in the context of RTT-sensitive congestion control algorithms. No specific citations are available from the supplied source metadata.
proposal.alternatives: The observed difference (or lack thereof) could reflect CCA-specific RTT sensitivity rather than a general delay effect; bottleneck buffer size may interact with delay to produce bufferbloat artifacts; transfer size may dominate completion time, masking delay effects for large files.
proposal.design: Independent-groups pilot: each replication is an independent netem invocation with two clients. Condition A (0 ms) and Condition B (20 ms) are run as separate configurations, each replicated 8 times, for 16 planned units total. Flow completion time in ms is recorded per client per replication.
proposal.metrics: Primary metric: flow_completion_time_ms per client flow. Comparison: distribution of completion times across 8 replications per condition, reported as median and range. No inferential interval is declared without a justified independent sampling design.
proposal.controls: Bottleneck rate, bottleneck buffer, CCA, file size, number of clients, and snapshot interval are held constant. Only the client_delays_ms parameter differs between conditions.
proposal.falsification: The pilot is falsified (no detectable effect) if the distributions of flow_completion_time_ms for 0 ms and 20 ms delay overlap completely across all 16 replications, with no consistent directional shift. A consistent directional shift in medians supports the claim but does not establish causality or generalization.
proposal.inputs: Built-in netem runner (emulated-netem-v1) with script netem_nines.py (requires exactly 2 clients). Source sha256: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa. Delay placement (one-way vs. round-trip), file size, and CCA remain unresolved pending owner answers.
proposal.limitations: This is a simulation pilot, not a real-world measurement. Results apply only to the specific emulated topology and chosen parameters. The pilot cannot resolve the broader claim across CCAs, file sizes, or real network conditions. Directionality of delay is unresolved and materially affects RTT and thus completion time.

cases.judgment: Declares independent invocations without an established sampling design and uses completely overlapping distributions as falsification/no detectable effect; protocol remains null, preventing execution.

output.summary: The paper claims 99.99% availability for a LEO optical-link terminal. No hardware, orbital trace, or full paper text is available. This draft identifies the key missing inputs (link-budget parameters, pass geometry, atmospheric model, and availability definition) and proposes a simulation-based independent check once those are resolved. Protocol is null pending three owner clarifications.
questions: What is the precise operational definition of 'availability' used in the paper — is it fraction of total LEO pass time with link margin above threshold, fraction of passes with at least one successful contact, or another metric, and what link-margin threshold (dB) applies?

Which atmospheric/weather impairment model and orbital parameters (altitude km, inclination °, ground-station latitude/longitude, minimum elevation angle °) does the paper use to derive the 99.99% figure?

Is a simulation tool, link-budget spreadsheet, or orbital-propagation script (e.g., STK, MATLAB, or open-source equivalent) referenced or available that could be used for an independent check, and if so, what version and configuration file hashes can be supplied?

proposal.problem: A LEO optical-link terminal is claimed to achieve 99.99% availability over LEO passes, but no hardware, orbital trace, atmospheric model, or full paper text is available to verify or reproduce this figure.
proposal.question: Under what orbital geometry, atmospheric impairment model, and link-budget assumptions does the proposed optical-link terminal achieve 99.99% availability over LEO passes, and can those assumptions be independently reproduced?
proposal.hypothesis: The proposed optical-link terminal maintains 99.99 percent availability over LEO passes.
proposal.conditions: Conditions are unresolved: orbital altitude, inclination, ground-station location, minimum elevation angle, link-margin threshold, and atmospheric/cloud-cover model are all unknown from the supplied metadata alone.
proposal.related_work: LEO optical-link availability analyses typically rely on orbital propagation (e.g., SGP4), atmospheric attenuation models (e.g., ITU-R P.1621), and cloud-cover statistics. No specific cited prior work is available from the supplied metadata.
proposal.alternatives: Alternative explanations for a 99.99% figure include: (a) availability defined over a single favorable ground station with low cloud cover; (b) diversity combining across multiple ground stations; (c) a narrow definition of 'pass' that excludes low-elevation contacts; or (d) an optimistic atmospheric model. These remain untested hypotheses.
proposal.design: An independent-check simulation would re-run the paper's orbital and link-budget model with identical parameters, then vary key assumptions (cloud cover, elevation mask, link margin) to assess sensitivity. Without the paper's model inputs, only a structural audit of the claim is possible at this stage.
proposal.metrics: Primary metric: fraction of LEO pass time (or fraction of passes) with received optical power above the stated link-margin threshold, expressed as a percentage. Secondary metric: sensitivity of availability to ±5 dB link-margin variation and ±10° elevation-mask variation.
proposal.controls: Baseline control: availability computed under clear-sky, zero-loss conditions (upper bound). Negative control: availability under median global cloud-cover statistics (lower bound). Both controls bracket the claimed 99.99% figure.
proposal.falsification: The claim is falsified if an independent simulation using the paper's stated parameters yields availability below 99.99% under the paper's own atmospheric and orbital assumptions. It is also falsified if the 99.99% figure is only achievable under conditions not disclosed in the paper (e.g., multi-site diversity not mentioned in the claim).
proposal.inputs: Required but missing: (1) orbital parameters (altitude, inclination, RAAN); (2) ground-station coordinates and minimum elevation angle; (3) link-budget parameters (transmit power, aperture, wavelength, pointing loss, detector sensitivity); (4) atmospheric/cloud model and geographic scope; (5) availability definition and threshold. Source SHA-256: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa.
proposal.limitations: No hardware access, no orbital trace, and no full paper text are available. The source is retrieved-unreviewed synthetic metadata only. Any simulation would be an independent check of the paper's model, not a real-world measurement. Results cannot establish causality or generalize beyond the simulated scenario.

cases.judgment: Identifies missing equipment/inputs and simulation limits, but introduces an unsupplied standard reference, asserts median-cloud controls are a lower bound without support, and overstates simulation discrepancies as falsification.
